title: GitHub Examples
description: Small GitHub examples from the lessons. Each example links back to its explanation and practice task.

examples.title: Git and GitHub have different jobs
examples.description: Git records file history on a computer. GitHub hosts Git repositories and adds pages for collaboration. You can learn local Git without a GitHub account.
examples.code:
Local computer: edit files and record Git commits
GitHub repository: share selected commits and review proposed changes

examples.title: Find your way around a repository
examples.description: A GitHub repository page has areas for code and collaboration. Start with its README, then inspect the files and recent changes.
examples.code:
Code: files and README
Issues: problems and ideas
Pull requests: proposed code changes
Actions: configured automated runs

examples.title: Follow the GitHub Flow
examples.description: GitHub Flow is a lightweight way to work on changes. A focused branch and pull request let people inspect an idea before it joins the main branch.
examples.code: Create a branch -> make focused commits -> open a pull request -> review and check -> merge when ready

examples.title: Write an issue someone can reproduce
examples.description: A GitHub issue can record a bug or proposed task. A useful bug report gives steps, expected behaviour and actual behaviour.
examples.code:
Title: Search misses lowercase moon
Steps: type moon in the book search
Expected: Moon appears
Actual: no matching book appears

examples.title: Explain a pull request
examples.description: A pull request, often called a PR, proposes combining changes from one branch into another. Its description should explain the result for a reviewer.
examples.code:
Base branch: main
Head branch: fix-search-case
Problem: lowercase queries missed titles
Change: compare title and query in lowercase
Check: Moon and moon both match

examples.title: Use the Files changed view
examples.description: The Files changed view shows the difference a PR proposes. Review the actual lines and ask focused questions about behaviour and edge cases.
examples.code:
Old: title === query
New: title.toLowerCase() === query.toLowerCase()
Review question: should outside spaces also be ignored?

examples.title: Understand review outcomes
examples.description: A GitHub review may comment, approve or request changes. Project branch rules determine which reviews are required before merging.
examples.code:
Comment: asks a question or gives feedback
Approve: reviewer considers the change ready
Request changes: reviewer identifies work needed

examples.title: Read an Actions check
examples.description: GitHub Actions can run a workflow when code changes. A workflow is a configured set of jobs and steps. Its check reports whether those steps succeeded.
examples.code:
Workflow file: .github/workflows/check.yml
Job: test
Step: run the project test command
Result: passed

examples.title: Protect the main branch with rules
examples.description: Repository rules can require reviews or status checks before a branch accepts changes. This helps a team apply the same process consistently.
examples.code:
Worked rule plan for main:
Require a pull request
Require the test status check
Require a suitable review
Allow only intended people to bypass rules

examples.title: Fork a project or clone it
examples.description: A fork is a hosted repository linked to an upstream project. A clone is a local repository copy. A fork can hold proposed contributions without granting write access to upstream.
examples.code:
Upstream project -> your hosted fork
Hosted fork -> local clone
Local commits -> proposed change from the fork

examples.title: Explain a version with a release
examples.description: A Git tag names a specific point in history. A GitHub release can add notes and downloadable files around a tag.
examples.code:
Tag: v1.1.0
Release title: Search improvement
Notes: search now ignores letter case
Known limit: outside spaces are still significant

examples.title: Read the community files
examples.description: Community files help people use and contribute to a repository. A licence explains reuse conditions; other files describe participation and reporting.
examples.code:
README.md: purpose and setup
LICENSE: reuse conditions
CONTRIBUTING.md: how to propose a change
CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md: community behaviour
SECURITY.md: how to report a security issue if provided
